proposal.hypothesis: Li3PO4 is a wide-gap (~6 eV) insulating orthophosphate with fully oxidized P5+, so it should resist oxidation at the 4.0 V LiCoO2 interface and remain chemically compatible with the sulfide Li6PS5Cl electrolyte. It is a well-known protective coating for oxide cathodes, and its Li-rich composition should minimize interfacial Li-exchange penalties.

LiF is a very wide-gap (~7 eV) ionic insulator with fully reduced F-, so it should resist oxidation at 4.0 V vs Li and is chemically stable toward the sulfide Li6PS5Cl. Unlike Li3PO4, which showed a sulfide-driven decomposition penalty (P2O5/SCl4/SO2 products), LiF has no oxidizable P or S centers and is a known low-reactivity coating, so its contact penalty should be much smaller.
proposal.motivation: Li3PO4 (mp-aaaaauhx) was insulating with a 5.8 eV gap but had a contact penalty of 0.337 eV/non-Li atom (bin 16) from reaction with Li6PS5Cl, so acceptability was not met. This choice moves to a different, halide family to test whether a non-phosphate, fluoride chemistry avoids the sulfide reaction.

proposal.hypothesis: Li2O is the most Li-rich, fully reduced oxide (O2-, no oxidizable P or S centers), so it should have little driving force to oxidize the sulfide Li6PS5Cl, unlike Li3PO4 (P5+ oxidized the sulfide) and LiF (F- reacted to give S and SCl products). Its wide gap should keep it insulating, and it stays in the oxide family while avoiding the phosphate and fluoride chemistries already tested.

proposal.hypothesis: LiCl has the same halide anion as the Cl- in Li6PS5Cl, so it should have little driving force for anion exchange or redox with the sulfide. Its Li-rich, fully reduced composition avoids the P5+ and S-oxidation pathways that gave the Li3PO4 and LiF penalties. Its wide gap should keep it insulating, and its Cl- oxidation onset should sit near the 4.0 V limit, which is a risk to check.
